Hmmm... lots of issues wrapped up in that.

For starters, the two biggest leading causes of bankruptcy in the US are

  1. Medical bills (62%)

  2. Job loss (22%)

  3. Poor use of credit (15%)

  4. Divorce (8%)

  5. Unexpected disaster (7%)

Yes, those percentages are more than 100%. I assume they must be considering multifactor bankruptcies.

http://blogs.lawyers.com/2012/05/the-top-5-causes-of-bankruptcy/

So that kind of stuff can nail both the poor and middle class. I honestly don't think you can have the poor cover all of their health care expenses unless you are committed to letting people die or be severely disabled if they cannot afford it.

I think we have job loss reasonably covered except in times of economic crisis where jobs just might not be available even for those who are committed and look hard. But the US provided extensions for unemployment benefits when that occurred.

Poor credit use... that is a self inflicted problem. And I honestly think a quarter of Personal Finance should be a required course in High School.

Divorce... I think having one party drag out the other in a long drawn out legal battle is a problem that needs to be solved. Forced mediation? I don't know. But it is needlessly ruining people's lives.

Unexpected disaster... Homes & rental properties are generally insured. It is just not the contents inside that are covered.

Another consideration in the US is the poor mass transit system. There is normally something if you live in a city, but people in rural areas can have a tough time. But even in cities with poor mass transit, it can be an issue for some poor to obtain work if it isn't on a bus line.

So after looking at all of that, the next question is what is a decent standard of living. Government subsided housing requires 1 bedroom for every couple and child. So do most custody decrees. Not all families live that way. Mexican immigrants certainly make due with less. Our grand parents certainly made do with less. Perhaps we should look at lowering our minimum standards when someone else is footing the bill.

And then we have food for the poor. We have various food programs that provide "food stamp" cards so people can get whatever they want. And there are reports of people using it irresponsibly to order a crap load of delivery pizza and wings the first week and then have themselves and their children starving the rest of the month. Maybe we should do grocery baskets of economical food options. Dry beans, rice, instant milk, canned meat, canned veggies, canned fruit. Maybe not ideal, but if it is coming out of someone else's pocket, as they say beggars can't be choosers. And it might prevent the issue where kids go hungry due to poor management from certain parents.

OK. So we want the poor to sustain themselves. What about the mentally ill? The physically handicapped? The blind? There are certainly some cases where some people cannot provide for themselves no matter what. And then we have job loss during economic downturns where clearly not everyone can find work. Honestly, I kind of liked the Civilian Conservation Corps. They provided work, maybe not the best choice, but food, housing,clothing and worked on the US infrastructure. It taught job skills .I think that program needs to be brought back as a staple for the long term unemployed.

Those are just my thoughts off the top of my head.

ETA: Of course the next question after this is "what is effective?" "What programs get us the results we want for a reasonable cost?" The items I discussed above might not be the most effective.
